lead: Every thermodynamics problem starts with a decision: what is inside the boundary and what is outside. The stuff inside is the system; the rest is the surroundings. Once the boundary is drawn, we describe the system by its properties — temperature, pressure, volume, mass. These properties split into two classes. Extensive properties grow with the size of the system; intensive properties do not. The split decides what you may add, what you may look up in a table, and what you may hold constant. Plant design, steam tables and simulation software all rest on it.
prereq: You need: nothing beyond school physics and chemistry — mass, volume, temperature and pressure as measured quantities. The next chapter, 1.2, uses these terms for state and path functions.

blocks.text: Thermodynamics begins with a choice. You draw a real or imaginary surface and declare that everything inside is the system and everything outside is the surroundings. That surface is the boundary. It can be the inner wall of a reactor, the skin of a potato in an oven, or a bubble of steam in a pipe. It can be fixed or moving, real or imagined.

The boundary decides the type of system. A closed system (some syllabi call it a control mass) has no mass crossing the boundary, though heat and work may cross. A sealed cylinder of gas cooled in a fridge is closed. An open system (a control volume) has mass crossing the boundary: a pump, a turbine, a length of pipe, a cup of chai while you sip it. An isolated system has neither mass nor energy crossing. A perfectly insulated, rigid, sealed flask is the ideal case; no real flask is perfect.

items: Sketch the equipment and mark the boundary with a dashed line.
Ask: does mass cross the boundary? If yes, the system is open.
If no mass crosses, ask: does heat or work cross? If yes, the system is closed.
If neither mass nor energy crosses, the system is isolated — an ideal limit.

blocks.text: A phase is a region with uniform chemical composition and uniform physical properties. Ice and liquid water in a glass are two phases. Air is one phase even though it is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen and argon, because it is mixed at the molecular level.

A component is a chemically independent species. The number of components is the smallest number of species needed to describe the composition of every phase present. Pure water is one component. Water plus ethanol is two. Salt dissolved in water is still two components (salt and water), even though the salt splits into ions.

items: A homogeneous system has one phase throughout: superheated steam, brine, dry air.
A heterogeneous system has two or more phases with boundaries between them: wet steam in a boiler drum, oil floating on water.
One phase may contain many components; many phases may share one component.

blocks.text: Any measurable feature of the system is a property. The test for the two classes is a thought experiment: cut the system into two equal halves. An extensive property halves with the system. Mass m, volume V, amount of substance n, internal energy U, enthalpy H and entropy S are extensive. Two identical vessels joined together hold twice the volume and twice the mass of one. An intensive property does not change with size. Temperature T, pressure P, density ρ and molar volume do not halve; each half of a gas at 300 K is still at 300 K.

A ratio of two extensive properties is intensive. Density divides mass by volume, so the size cancels. Specific volume is volume per unit mass. Molar volume is volume per mole. Specific properties are per kilogram (lower-case symbols v, u, h, s). Molar properties are per mole. Both are intensive, which is why a steam table can list them without knowing the mass of the plant.
ρ = m/V,   v = V/m = 1/ρ,   V<sub>m</sub> = V/n
blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³; m is mass in kg; V is volume in m³; v is specific volume in m³/kg; V<sub>m</sub> is molar volume in m³/mol; n is amount of substance in mol.

blocks.text: The rule that catches students: extensive properties add, intensive properties never do. Join two 1 m³ tanks of water at 300 K and you get 2 m³ at 300 K, not 2 m³ at 600 K. Write m = m₁ + m₂ for masses, but never T = T₁ + T₂ for temperatures.

figure.caption: The boundary decides the system type: mass crossing makes it open; heat or work crossing alone keeps it closed; nothing crossing makes it isolated.

spec.aria: A tree classifies thermodynamic systems as closed, open and isolated by what crosses the boundary.

examples.question: A closed rigid vessel holds 2.0 kg of gas at 300 K and 150 kPa. Its volume is 1.2 m³. Classify m, V, T, P, density and specific volume as intensive or extensive. Compute the density and the specific volume.
steps: Data: mass m = 2.0 kg, volume V = 1.2 m³, temperature T = 300 K, pressure P = 150 kPa. The vessel is closed and rigid, so m is fixed.
Classify the simple variables: m and V grow when you take more gas, so both are extensive. T and P are the same everywhere inside and do not depend on how much gas is present, so both are intensive.
Density: ρ = m/V = 2.0 kg ÷ 1.2 m³ = 1.667 kg/m³. Mass per unit volume is a ratio of two extensives, so ρ is intensive.
Specific volume: v = V/m = 1.2 m³ ÷ 2.0 kg = 0.6 m³/kg. Volume per unit mass is also intensive.
Consistency check: v = 1/ρ = 1 ÷ 1.667 = 0.6 m³/kg. The two answers agree.
examples.answer: Density ρ = 1.667 kg/m³ and specific volume v = 0.6 m³/kg, both intensive; m and V are extensive, T and P are intensive.
examples.check:
m = 2.0
V = 1.2
rho = m / V
v = V / m
print(round(rho, 3))
print(round(v, 3))

traps: Density ρ = m/V and specific volume v = V/m are intensive even though they are built from the extensive m and V. A ratio of two extensives is intensive; do not label the ratio extensive because a big letter appears in the formula.

Intensive properties are not additive. Joining two vessels at 300 K and 400 K does not give 350 K; the final temperature depends on the masses and heat capacities, and the volumes add while the temperatures do not.
Closed means no mass crosses, not no energy. A closed vessel can still be heated or stirred. An insulated vessel is not automatically isolated unless no work crosses either.

The system is not the equipment. In a cylinder, the gas may be the system and the metal wall part of the surroundings; choose and state the boundary before naming anything, because the same gas can be closed in one problem and open in another.

quiz.q: Define system, surroundings and boundary in one line each.
quiz.a: System: the quantity of matter or region chosen for study. Surroundings: everything outside the system. Boundary: the real or imaginary surface separating them.

quiz.q: Name the three system types classified by what crosses the boundary, and say what crosses in each.
quiz.a: Closed (control mass): no mass crosses, heat and work may. Open (control volume): mass crosses. Isolated: neither mass nor energy crosses.

quiz.q: Density is defined as mass divided by volume, yet it is intensive. Explain why in two or three sentences.
quiz.a: Mass and volume are both extensive and both double when the system doubles. In the ratio m/V the factor of two cancels, so density stays the same. A ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.

quiz.q: A tank holds 0.8 m³ of a liquid of mass 640 kg. Find its density and specific volume, and state the class of each.
quiz.a: ρ = m/V = 640/0.8 = 800 kg/m³ (intensive). v = V/m = 0.8/640 = 0.00125 m³/kg = 1.25 × 10⁻³ m³/kg (intensive).

quiz.q: 5 mol of gas occupies 0.1 m³. Find the molar volume in m³/mol and in L/mol.
quiz.a: V<sub>m</sub> = V/n = 0.1/5 = 0.02 m³/mol. Since 1 m³ = 1000 L, this is 20 L/mol. Molar volume is intensive.

quiz.q: Two closed rigid vessels of equal volume hold the same gas, one at 300 K and one at 400 K. They are connected and mixed. A student writes T = 350 K. Is that justified by the property classes alone? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Temperature is intensive, so it cannot simply be averaged by volume or added. The final temperature follows from an energy balance using the masses and heat capacities, and equals 350 K only in the special case of equal masses of the same gas with constant heat capacity. The class of the property forbids adding or averaging it as a rule.

quiz.q: A sealed, perfectly insulated, rigid flask contains reacting chemicals. Is it isolated? Can its temperature change? Justify using the definitions.
quiz.a: Yes, it is isolated: no mass, no heat and no work cross the boundary. Its internal energy stays constant, but temperature can still rise or fall because chemical energy converts to thermal energy inside the system. Isolation fixes U, not T.

quiz.q: Give one homogeneous and one heterogeneous system from a power plant, and name the phases.
quiz.a: Homogeneous: superheated steam in a pipe, one phase. Heterogeneous: wet steam in the boiler drum, two phases — liquid water and water vapour.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every process simulator — Aspen Plus, DWSIM, HYSYS — asks you to declare a control volume first, then attaches intensive and extensive property sets to it. Battery thermal management and data-centre cooling models use the same split: temperature and pressure fields are intensive, while coolant mass and stored energy are extensive. Exergy analysis in Unit 3 keeps the distinction when it separates lost work from stored energy.
